metadata.title: Estimating Cross-Country Investment in Training: An Experimental Methodology Using PIAAC Data
metadata.venue: OECD Science, Technology and Industry Working Papers

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses microdata from the OECD Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) 2012 (fielded over 2011–2012) and links it to external Labour Force Survey (LFS) and System of National Accounts (SNA) information to construct economy- and industry-level investment estimates for 22 OECD countries. Because the PIAAC target population and employment structure differ from LFS/SNA reference populations (e.g., age-group differences and country coverage such as Belgium/UK subnational coverage), the authors recalibrate PIAAC sampling weights to make the resulting statistics representative at the country and industry levels. They winsorise key input variables at the 1% and 99% percentiles to limit outlier-driven measurement error, and they compute new weights using the generalised regression estimator (GREG) approach (Deville and Särndal, 1992) with auxiliary variables including age, gender, employment status, and (for the employed) sector, occupation, and wages by industry plus employment in working hours. The paper does not report a specific single weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT) nor replicate-weight methodology, so the exact weight variable used in the final calculations cannot be extracted from the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper is a data-linking and measurement methodology for expenditure-based investment in training (formal, on-the-job, and informal learning) aggregated to country and industry levels; it does not model cognitive achievement outcomes with PIAAC plausible values. Missing-data handling is not described as a formal statistical procedure (e.g., listwise deletion or multiple imputation) for an ML estimation task, so the specific approach to missingness in inputs (e.g., wages, training responses, or linked external variables) is not documented in the provided text. This is therefore a reporting gap relative to what would be needed to fully reproduce the measurement pipeline under missingness.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis is based on PIAAC 2012 microdata (fielded over 2011–2012) linked to LFS and SNA data to estimate training investment for 22 OECD countries at economy and industry levels. The paper restricts the training investment estimation to individuals in employment at the moment of the interview (excluding unemployed/inactive for the main investment calculations) to produce industry- or occupation-specific estimates. It excludes the Russian Federation from the analysis due to difficulties constructing representative weights excluding the Moscow region. For public-sector estimates, it further restricts the population to individuals working in public entities within specified non-market industries (ISIC Rev.4 sectors 72 and 84–93). For formal training, it uses the highest level of schooling attended in the last 12 months as a proxy for formal education, and it notes that pk and qk weights are missing for Japan in some sectors and are addressed by borrowing Korean sector responses in the same four-digit sector.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper proposes an experimental, expenditure-based methodology to measure cross-country investment in human capital via workforce training, using PIAAC microdata linked to Labour Force Surveys and System of National Accounts. It distinguishes three training types—formal training, on-the-job training, and informal learning—and estimates both opportunity costs (foregone work/leisure time) and direct costs (employer/worker cost shares), discounted using PIAAC responses on training allocation and perceived usefulness. The approach produces comparable economy- and industry-level investment estimates for 22 OECD countries for 2011–2012, and also provides first-time estimates for private vs public sectors. Results indicate that average total investment in training is about 6.7% of gross value added (GVA), with on-the-job training around 2.4% of GVA on average, and substantial heterogeneity by country and sector. The paper validates robustness by recomputing the capitalisation factors (p and q) under alternative assumptions and reports very high rank correlations across methodologies, while noting limitations such as reliance on wage measures not assumed to equal marginal products and the need for further work to build time-series capital stock estimates.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a measurement/methodology and descriptive estimation paper rather than an ML predictive study: it does not train or evaluate machine-learning models, and it does not report a student-level predictive target with performance metrics. Consequently, fields such as total_students, per-country n_students, and ML technique lists are not fully extractable from the provided text, and main_findings are intentionally left empty because the schema requires StructuredFinding rows only for empirical ML/predictive outcomes.
